claims.text: SQUID magnetometry can reveal a ferromagnetic ground state.
A ferromagnetic ground state can be identified by a low-temperature hysteresis loop in magnetization versus applied magnetic field.
The sample has unknown magnetic ordering and lacks clear macroscopic magnetic characterization.
The magnetic field should be varied across a range of temperatures, particularly below the estimated Curie temperature.
Controlled field sweeps below the Curie temperature can detect magnetic hysteresis.
Alignment of magnetic moments in the crystalline lattice mediates long-range ferromagnetic ordering.
Exchange interactions produce spontaneous magnetic ordering in a ferromagnetic ground state.
Spontaneous ferromagnetic ordering leads to measurable hysteresis in the magnetization-field curve.
A low-temperature hysteresis loop with nonzero remanent magnetization and coercive field indicates ferromagnetic behavior.
A paramagnet typically has a linear, reversible magnetization response without hysteresis.
Measurements above the Curie point should show no hysteresis and a reversible magnetization response.
Sufficient sample homogeneity and sufficiently low defect levels are required for ferromagnetic domains to form and be detected.
Weak magnetic ordering can make SQUID magnetometry results ambiguous.
Substrate interactions can complicate magnetic measurements of thin films.
Sample inhomogeneities can mask or mimic a ferromagnetic hysteresis signal.
Absence of remanence and coercivity in low-temperature magnetization-field curves would falsify the proposed ferromagnetic ground state.

contradictions.description: The boundary and uncertainty fields acknowledge that weak ordering, defects, inhomogeneity, or thin-film effects may mask a genuine ferromagnetic signal, whereas the falsification rule treats absence of hysteresis, remanence, and coercivity as falsifying the ferromagnetic ground state. Thus a negative result is not necessarily decisive under the stated boundaries.
